Issue Reading note
One reportable segment, no franchise P&L The chief operating decision maker is the CEO and reviews consolidated net income (10-K FY2026, Note 14). Every custom-versus-merchant revenue and margin figure here is triangulated from earnings-call commentary and tagged [estimate: …] with its range. The 10-K supports only the qualitative statement that "the percentage of our sales related to custom or semi-custom products has been increasing over the last few years"
The latest printed quarter has no 10-Q Q2 FY2027 was reported one day before the run date. Customer concentration, purchase commitments, the Google warrant's grant-date fair value and the Celestial AI earnout mark are all one quarter old, on series that have been moving fast: the largest distributor went from 37% of FY2026 revenue to 45% in Q1 FY2027
End-market recast and a divestiture inside the same year Enterprise networking, carrier infrastructure, consumer and automotive/industrial were merged into one "communications and other" line in Q4 FY2026, so the four-way split ends with FY2025. The automotive Ethernet business sold to Infineon on 2025-08-14 stayed in continuing operations to the close date, and its $1,830m pre-tax gain is booked in interest income and other, outside operating income. Prior years were not restated
A dated reset of the forward framework Management said on 2026-08-27 that it will "reset that long-term target model" at an Investor Day in New York on 2026-10-06, five weeks after the run date. The dormant 64–66% gross-margin target, the FY2029 custom revenue target and the CY2028 market-size estimate are all expected to move there
  • GAAP and non-GAAP diverge more widely at Marvell than at any silicon peer in the comparable set. Amortization of acquired intangibles was $942m and stock-based compensation $591m in FY2026, against $8,195m of revenue. Consensus FY2027 non-GAAP EPS is $4.17 against GAAP $2.10.
  • Roughly $22bn of acquisition consideration has been spent since 2018 and no goodwill has ever been impaired, because Marvell tests goodwill as a single reporting unit whose fair value is its own market capitalization, so no deal-level return record exists (§11).

1. Business description, model and unit economics

Marvell designs high-speed analog, mixed-signal and DSP silicon and has it manufactured by others. It owns no fabs. One intellectual-property block appears in almost everything it sells: the ultra-high-speed SerDes that moves bits across a package, a board, a cable or a fibre.▪ The 10-K describes the custom ASIC platform as built on "a broad suite of differentiated Marvell intellectual property including ultra-high-speed SerDes, ARM compute, security, storage, silicon photonics and advanced packaging" (10-K FY2026, Item 1), and the same SerDes appears inside optical DSPs, PCIe retimers, active-electrical-cable DSPs, Teralynx switches and the scale-up fabrics in development.

Two end markets are reported. FY2026 revenue was $8,194.6m: data center $6,100.3m and communications and other $2,094.3m (10-K FY2026, Note 3). In the quarter ended 2026-08-01 the split was $2,171.5m and $567.8m, so data center reached 79% of revenue.▪

Source: 10-K FY2026 Note 3 and 10-K FY2025 Note 3, in millions. Communications and other for FY2024 and FY2025 is the sum of the four end markets reported separately until the Q4 FY2026 recast.

Underneath the data-center line are two businesses with different economics. Custom silicon is designed to one hyperscaler's specification and sold only to that customer. Everything else in data center is a standard product sold to many buyers. The filings do not separate them. Management put custom revenue at approximately $1.5bn for FY2026, "doubled" year over year, on the Q4 FY2026 call (2026-03-05), which is 18.3% of company revenue and 24.6% of the data-center line.▪ The residual, roughly $4,600m, is the merchant data-center franchise [estimate: disclosed FY2026 data-center revenue less management's $1.5bn custom figure].

1.1 Data center — custom silicon

Custom AI accelerators ("XPUs") plus an attach portfolio around them: custom network interface controllers, CXL memory expanders and near-memory compute, custom storage controllers, memory interface controllers and security co-processors. The buyer is a hyperscaler silicon team choosing between designing in-house on a physical-design service, buying full-service custom from Marvell, Broadcom, Alchip, GUC, MediaTek or Socionext, or staying on merchant GPUs.

The economic unit is a design-win socket. At the June 2025 custom-silicon event Murphy sized the two kinds: "these XPU programs are monsters. They're typically multibillion dollars in lifetime revenue each, and they run between an 18- and 24-month period… When you look at the XPU attach programs… these are in the several hundred million dollars in lifetime revenue, but they span over a 2- to 4-year period." Eighteen sockets were disclosed at that date — five XPU and thirteen attach, twelve of them at the top four US hyperscalers — against a pipeline of more than 50 opportunities across more than ten customers worth $75bn of claimed lifetime revenue▪ [deck: Custom AI Investor Event 2025-06-17, slides 22–23].

The attach split is Murphy's own on the Q4 FY2026 call: "XPU attached probably in the couple of hundred million ballpark say like this last year, doubling this year, maybe over doubling again the year after."

Reported non-GAAP gross margin of 59.5% (Q4 FY2026 call) equals one minus $3,322.8m of Note 14 product cost over $8,194.6m of revenue, which confirms that the Note 14 line is the non-GAAP cost of goods sold. The reconstruction above reproduces that product-cost total to within 0.02%, and it does so by construction: the merchant margin was chosen so the identity closes, so the reconciliation is a consistency check and not independent evidence for the split.

Three approaches give different answers for the custom margin. Solving the disclosed non-GAAP gross margin against management's custom revenue for the FY2025–FY2026 pair gives 34.9% custom and 65.0% merchant; the FY2024–FY2025 pair gives 59.6%; the FY2024–FY2026 pair gives 49.9%. The most recent pair, in which merchant mix moved least, is the most usable. Varying the assumed FY2026 merchant margin from 63.0% to 66.0% moves implied custom from 43.7% to 30.1%. The Q3 FY2027 guide is a third check: revenue rises from $2,739.3m to a $3,150m midpoint while non-GAAP gross margin declines from 58.9% to 58.0%, an incremental 51.9%, and the CFO named the cause — "Part of the acceleration story in Q3, as you point out, mix is the primary driver. We've got a strong ramp in custom" (Q2 FY2027 call). The usable answer is a range: custom 30–44%, centred near 35–39%; merchant 63–66% [estimate: mix algebra on disclosed consolidated non-GAAP gross margins and management's custom revenue figures].▪

Pure-play design houses set the floor. Alchip's FY2025 gross margin was 26%, up from 20% in 2024, and Global Unichip ran 21.5% in the June 2026 quarter on a turnkey-heavy mix [web]. Marvell earns more because it contributes its own SerDes, dense SRAM, die-to-die and packaging blocks instead of only physical design and supply-chain management.▪

What passes through the cost line, and what does not. The common framing is that custom margins are low because Marvell resells high-bandwidth memory. Koopmans said the opposite at the June 2025 event: "when we work with the very largest hyperscalers in the world, what they tell us is that they want to buy the HBM directly… Now emerging hyperscalers, they might want to get a turnkey service from Marvell… But just to be conservative, we're going to take that out of our TAM." Marvell's own market slides apply the same exclusion, breaking the CY2028 accelerated-compute market into $163bn of XPU, $58bn of XPU attach and $128bn of HBM attach, then taking 25% of the roughly $220bn ex-HBM figure to reach a $55.4bn custom market [deck: 2025-06-17, slides 38–40]. What does pass through Marvell's cost of goods sold is the wafer, the CoWoS interposer, the advanced substrate and the assembly and test, because Marvell sells the full service. Marvell's "custom HBM" is a design-IP product, a base logic die that moves memory controllers off the compute die and releases 1.7x more compute area [deck: 2025-06-17, slide 97].

Contract structure. Purchase orders refreshed annually. The 10-K states it plainly: "We typically sell products pursuant to purchase orders rather than long-term purchase commitments." Note 3 elects the practical expedient that removes disclosure of unsatisfied performance obligations for contracts under one year, which covers the custom book, so no backlog line appears anywhere in the filings. What management gives instead is purchase-order coverage: "we have purchased orders covering the entirety of this fiscal year's forecast for this next-generation program" (Q4 FY2026 call) and "we already have firm requirements in place for all of next fiscal year" on the second Tier-1 program (Q1 FY2027 call). The $75bn pipeline and the $120bn Google warrant threshold describe opportunity; roughly one year of it is under order at any time.

Customer-funded engineering. Non-recurring engineering receipts are booked as a reduction of operating expense. Koopmans, June 2025: "our customers sort of co-invest and we recognize that as a reduction in our operating expense… the actual investment is actually quite a bit larger than is shown on our P&L." Custom revenue is product revenue only, and custom's operating-margin gap to merchant is narrower than the roughly 26-point gross-margin gap by an amount no filing sizes.▪ Management's claim is that custom programs are "extremely accretive to operating margin and operating income at the bottom line level" despite the lower gross margin (Q2 FY2025 call). That claim cannot be tested against any reported figure.

Customer warrants reduce revenue. Three are outstanding. A FY2025 warrant covers up to 4.2m shares at $87.77, grant-date fair value $54.44 per share and $227.6m in total, of which 0.7m had vested at 2026-01-31; a FY2026 warrant covers 1.0m shares at $87.00 at $53.02 per share, none vested (10-K FY2026, Note 3). The Google warrant, issued 2026-08-18 under a commercial agreement dated 2026-07-29, covers 58,970,907 shares at $206.58: 1,360,867 vest on time and the remaining 57,610,040 vest in 240 equal tranches of 240,042 shares, one per $500m of Custom Products revenue, through the end of FY2033 (8-K filed 2026-08-19).▪ All three "are recognized as a reduction to revenue as qualifying revenues are recognized during the vesting term."

The rate is calculable within a band. The two disclosed warrants price at 62.0% and 60.9% of their strikes; applied to $206.58 that is $126 to $128 per share, so each tranche costs about $30m against $500m of revenue, or 6.0%–6.2%. Black-Scholes on the disclosed 8-K terms at 35%–60% volatility gives $99 to $137 per share, a wider 4.7%–6.6%. The realized analogue points to the top of both bands: FY2026 recorded $39.0m of contra-revenue against 0.6m of vesting FY2025-warrant shares, about $65 per share on an $87.77 strike, or 74% of strike. The usable range is roughly 5% to 8% of qualifying Google revenue, and $6bn to $10bn of grant-date fair value for the full 58.97m shares [estimate: the two prior warrants' disclosed fair-value-to-strike ratios, plus Black-Scholes on the 8-K terms at 35%–60% volatility]. At a 35% pre-warrant custom gross margin, the 5% to 8% band takes the reported margin on Google programs to between about 31% and about 29%, and the realized analogue points to the lower figure.▪

Data center is guided to grow about 60% and interconnect above 70%, while custom's written guide is "more than 20%". A business driven by hyperscaler AI capex would grow with the rest of data center. Custom needs roughly $2.4bn, or +60%, merely to hold its 25% share of data-center revenue; at the written guide it declines to about 19%. Custom added roughly $1,500m of the $2,275m company revenue increase from FY2023 to FY2026, about 66%; on the FY2027 guide it adds between $300m and $1,000m of a $3,805m increase, 8% to 26%. The line that inflected in FY2027 is merchant interconnect.

Capital. Being fabless does not make growth here low-cost in cash terms. FY2026 capital expenditure was $354.1m, 4.3% of revenue, and management plans roughly $1bn of supplier capacity prepayments in FY2027. Disclosed unconditional purchase commitments to foundries and test-and-assembly partners were $2,665.8m at 2026-01-31 with $1,871.8m due inside FY2027 (10-K FY2026, Note 8). Work-in-process was 80% of the $1,388.0m inventory balance, up from 69%, which is what a shift toward long-cycle advanced-node and advanced-package builds produces. The cash is paid twelve to twenty-four months before the revenue: Durn attributed the sequential decline in Q2 FY2027 operating cash flow to "the higher capacity prepayments to suppliers in support of Marvell's future growth."

1.2 Data center — interconnect and merchant silicon

The standard-product half of data center, and the largest franchise in the company at roughly 56% of FY2026 revenue. Four product families make it up.

Interconnect PAM4, coherent and coherent-lite optical DSPs; silicon-germanium trans-impedance amplifiers and laser drivers; silicon photonics; COLORZ data-center-interconnect pluggable modules; linear-pluggable-optics chipsets; active-electrical-cable DSPs; PCIe retimers ~2,880
Merchant Ethernet switching Teralynx (to 51.2T) and Prestera switch silicon; Alaska PHYs; controllers and adapters ~320

Management's own decomposition is coarser and comes from calls: interconnect is "roughly half our overall data center revenue", custom "roughly 1/4", and "the remaining quarter of our data center business which includes storage, switching and other products" (Q3 FY2026 call). Three sub-lines have been sized directly: data-center-interconnect modules at roughly $500m in FY2026 with line of sight to $1bn annualized during FY2028; trans-impedance amplifiers and drivers exceeding a $1bn annualized run rate "in the next few quarters"; and scale-out switching above $300m in FY2026, guided above $600m in FY2027 and toward $1bn annualized in FY2028 (Q4 FY2026 and Q1 FY2027 calls). Three franchises approaching $1bn each is the current shape of a $4.6bn segment.

The payer is usually not the hyperscaler. For interconnect the invoice goes to an optical module maker (Innolight, Eoptolink, Coherent, Lumentum, Fabrinet), a cable maker (Amphenol, TE Connectivity, Luxshare) or the ODM building the switch. The hyperscaler's network architecture team specifies the DSP by part number during qualification and then buys the finished module.▪ Marvell describes the mechanism directly for active electrical cables: the Golden Cable programme supplies "validated reference designs, enabling ecosystem partners to rapidly design and deploy AEC products at scale" (Q4 FY2026 call). Two exceptions: Marvell sells the finished data-center-interconnect module itself, so that payer is closer to the network operator; and for storage the payers are the drive makers, with the 10-K stating Bravera HDD controllers "are being used by all the current HDD makers."

Why a customer picks Marvell. First-to-market cadence at each speed generation. A module maker qualifies a DSP roughly twelve to eighteen months before volume [estimate: the realized 1.6T interval, qualification under way by May 2024 against production in the second half of FY2026; the 10-K says only "several months or more"], so whoever ships a working part first wins the generation. Marvell was first with 100G-per-lane (800G) and first to productize 200G-per-lane (1.6T), and demonstrated 400G-per-lane at OFC in April 2025.▪ Trade estimates put Marvell at about 60% of the 400G-and-above PAM4 optical DSP market with Broadcom above 30%▪ (eu.36kr.com, accessed 2026-08-28) [web]; a second source puts Marvell nearer 70% (bepresearch.substack.com, accessed 2026-08-28) [web, unverified]. Neither names a research firm and the ten-point gap is not resolvable from the filings.

The switch-silicon row cannot be built even at low precision. A bottom-up cost build on the 51.2T part, which has "more than 60 billion transistors" on Marvell 5nm [deck 2024-04-11, slide 93], puts silicon cost near $550 at a $18,500 wafer price and roughly 34 good die per wafer. A top-down port build gives a different answer: at a $3,000 ASP the disclosed FY2026 revenue implies more than 100,000 chips and roughly 6.4m 800G switch ports, against an 800G module market of 18–24m ports in CY2025, which would be a 27%–36% port share for a supplier holding roughly 4% of the switch-silicon market. The two approaches differ by more than 3x on units and neither can be reconciled from public material.

The build reconciles to the reported consolidated margin. Segment gross profit of $2,939m at 63.9%, plus custom at $630m and communications at $1,257m, totals $4,826m against $4,876m of reported non-GAAP gross profit. The residual is $50m, or 0.6 points of consolidated gross margin.

Price, volume and cost. No long-term price contracts are disclosed and the 10-K commits to the opposite: "We expect that the average unit selling prices of our products will continue to be subject to significant pricing pressures. In order to offset expected declines in the selling prices of our products, we will need to continue to introduce innovative new products and attempt to reduce the cost to design and manufacture our products." The gap between list and realized price appears in one balance-sheet line: variable-consideration estimates of $713.8m in accrued liabilities at 2026-01-31, 8.7% of FY2026 revenue held back for price protection, discounts, rebates and stock rotation (10-K FY2026, Note 15). Realized price rises only across a generation transition — a 1.6T DSP prices at roughly twice an 800G part for twice the lane rate — and declines every year within a generation. Cost is wafer, substrate, package and test, and leading-edge wafer prices are rising: 5nm at roughly $18,500, 3nm at $20,000 and 2nm near $30,000 in 2026 [web].

The relationship between this segment and custom. Custom pays for its own engineering — "NRE is treated as contra OpEx" (Q4 FY2025 call) — and reuses the IP this segment paid to build. The consequence is that ranking the two franchises on gross margin alone does not settle which earns more at the operating line, and the operating line cannot be computed because NRE is not sized in any filing.

The communications gross margin is derived by decomposing reported consolidated non-GAAP gross margin against disclosed end-market mix across three windows, which give 66.3%, 70.5% and 74.6%.▪ The nine-point spread comes from a confound the disclosure cannot remove: custom-versus-merchant mix inside data center moved at the same time as end-market mix, and management attributes the FY2027 margin path to custom specifically. Longer windows over-attribute the decline to end-market mix and overstate the communications margin. Demand drivers. Enterprise networking reduces to campus Ethernet switch, wireless access point and branch router units shipped by Cisco, HPE, Extreme, Ubiquiti and the Chinese OEMs, with content per port rising through the Wi-Fi 6E to Wi-Fi 7 transition as multi-gigabit PHY ports enter the access switch. Carrier reduces to 5G baseband and radio units at Nokia and Samsung, Marvell's two named OCTEON Fusion customers, plus coherent transport and broadband-access ports. Consumer reduces to console build schedules ahead of the holiday: FY2026 consumer ran $63.1m, $115.9m, $116.6m and about $84m across the four quarters, which is a build-schedule pattern.

Over FY2023 to FY2026 this franchise subtracted $1,416.5m of revenue while the company added $2,275.0m. All four sub-drivers contributed negatively. The realized driver over that window was the channel inventory cycle, amplified by sell-in accounting on 43% of FY2026 revenue: enterprise networking declined 49% in FY2025 against a campus switch market that contracted 20% in 2024, roughly 2.5x the amplitude of the market it sells into.▪ Management's stated forward drivers — enterprise IT spending and carrier capital expenditure — were not the realized drivers. Content growth is a hypothesis here: it has not appeared in three years of reported numbers, and management's own definition of a fully normalized enterprise networking business, "approximately $1 billion in annualized revenue" in Q4 FY2026 described as "the complete normalization of customer inventory levels", is 27% below the FY2023 print of $1,369.2m.

2. Key technologies and technical differentiators

Marvell has one deep technical asset and sells it in about a dozen packages: the same intellectual property produces market leadership in one socket and low-single-digit share in another.

224G and 112G SerDes. A SerDes converts parallel on-chip data into a single high-rate serial stream and recovers it at the far end through equalization, clock recovery and forward error correction. The line rate per lane sets the bandwidth of every interface built on it. A 224G lane closing timing at 50dB of channel loss requires analog front-end, data converter and DSP co-design at the edge of CMOS device physics, and the design has to be re-proven at every process node. Marvell's process-enablement work shows three to four years from a foundry process becoming available, through test-chip IP validation, to a shipped product [deck: 2025-06-17, slide 76]. The evidence that this is hard is that three companies sell high-end PAM4 DSPs at all — Marvell, Broadcom and, from March 2026, Credo — and the first two hold more than 90% of the 400G-and-above market [web]. Marvell demonstrated 400G-per-lane at 224 Gbaud at OFC in April 2025 and calls a related part "the world's first 448G electrical and optical SerDes" [deck: 2025-06-17, slide 25]; the press releases from the same period describe 400G-per-lane and a joint 450G-per-lane demonstration, so three numbers describe adjacent claims about one generation.

PAM4 optical DSPs. PAM4 encodes two bits per symbol, doubling throughput at a given baud rate at the cost of a much smaller eye opening, which is what the DSP's equalization, clock recovery, carrier recovery, forward error correction and coded modulation exist to recover. The Ara 1.6T part is built on TSMC 3nm, integrates eight 200Gbps electrical and eight 200Gbps optical lanes and enables modules under 22W [web]. Marvell was first to productize 200G-per-lane; 1.6T entered production in the second half of FY2026 and is ramping through FY2027, and the 800G platform entered its fifth year of production in FY2026 with demand still accelerating. Management's stated reason for durability is sequencing: consistent execution "enables us to secure qualifications at major customers well ahead of competitors" (Q3 FY2026 call). The lead is measured in quarters. Broadcom announced and began sampling a monolithic 3nm 400G-per-lane DSP on 2026-03-11 while Marvell's competing coherent parts were expected to sample in the second half of 2026 (futurumgroup.com, accessed 2026-08-28) [web].

Silicon-germanium trans-impedance amplifiers and drivers. A TIA converts photodiode current to voltage on the receive side; a driver swings the modulator on the transmit side. These are bipolar silicon-germanium parts on a different process from the CMOS DSP, held since the Inphi acquisition. Management describes "a significant market share and content" in them and expects a $1bn annualized run rate within a few quarters (Q1 and Q2 FY2027 calls). This is the one Marvell technology that survives every outcome in the pluggable-versus-co-packaged debate: DSP-based pluggables need it, linear pluggable optics chipsets are "optimized TIAs and laser drivers" (10-K FY2026, Item 1), near-package optics needs it, and linear-drive co-packaged optics needs it.▪

Coherent, coherent-lite and data-center-interconnect modules. Coherent DSPs recover amplitude and phase, allowing transmission over hundreds to thousands of kilometres; coherent-lite strips the power budget down for 2–20km campus links. Marvell has shipped more than a million DCI modules on its own silicon photonics over the past decade and accumulated more than 15 billion hours of field data across four generations (Q1 FY2027 call), announced the first secure 1.6T ZR and ZR+ modules on a 2nm coherent DSP on 2026-03-05, and added plasmonic modulators through the Polariton acquisition announced 2026-04-22. Distance physics keeps coherent modulation necessary at these reaches, so the substitution risk here is weaker than in the pluggable DSP business.

Silicon photonics and the light engine. Silicon photonics integrates waveguides, modulators, photodetectors, drivers, TIAs and microcontrollers onto a CMOS-fabricated die, so an optical interface can be built in a high-volume logic fab. Marvell's own 6.4T 3D silicon-photonics engine, 32 lanes of 224G optical, was announced in December 2023 and demonstrated at OFC in successive years (marvell.com, accessed 2026-08-28) [web]. Murphy described it in August 2026 as "our own organically developed solution, which we call our light engine, which we've been in development on for several years, and we've shown it off at OFC for several years." No revenue has been disclosed for it. Marvell then agreed on 2025-12-02 to buy Celestial AI, closing 2026-02-02 for total purchase consideration of $3,537m, and every dollar of disclosed co-packaged-optics revenue forecast originates with the acquired company. The distinction that matters is that the fifteen billion field-hours are DCI — long-reach, low-lane-count, board-edge coherent optics — while the scale-up problem is high-density short-reach optics running inside the thermal envelope of a multi-kilowatt accelerator. Marvell's own description of what Celestial adds is thermal stability sufficient to co-package photonics vertically in a 3D package with the accelerator instead of at the die edge (Q3 FY2026 call).

Photonic Fabric. A chiplet integrating drivers, TIAs, equalizers, SerDes, microcontrollers, modulators, photodiodes and waveguides, co-packaged into both the accelerator and the scale-up switch so the optical link terminates on the compute die. Claimed at 16 Tbps of first-generation bandwidth, above 2x the power efficiency of copper (Q3 FY2026 call), with a second-generation link claimed at 30x the reach of passive copper, 4x bandwidth, 4x lower power and 4x lower latency at roughly the same cost [deck: 2026-03-05, slide 10]. The two disclosures use different generations and different power multiples for the same comparison. One design win exists, at a Tier 1 hyperscaler, and nothing has shipped in volume.

Merchant Ethernet switching. Teralynx is a programmable cloud switch architecture acquired with Innovium in 2021, at capacities to 51.2Tbps and beyond; Prestera covers 12Gbps to 12.8Tbps for enterprise and carrier. Marvell reached each capacity generation well after Broadcom.

Capacity Broadcom Marvell Gap to volume
51.2T Tomahawk 5 shipping 2022 Teralynx 10 announced spring 2023, sampling Q2 FY2024, strong ramp only in FY2027 ~3 years
102.4T Tomahawk 6 announced 2025-06-03, production volume 2026-03-12 Teralynx T100 announced 2026-06-01, sampling Q2 CY2026, volume targeted mid-2027 ~12–15 months

Sources: Q1/Q2 FY2024 and Q4 FY2026 calls for Marvell; investors.broadcom.com, accessed 2026-08-28 [web] for Broadcom. The differentiation claim here is not a lead. Murphy's framing is a barrier-to-entry argument: "there's been a lot of companies that have tried and failed to do these [reticle] size very complex Ethernet switches, and it's only getting harder with the SerDes performance and the speeds" (Q2 FY2027 call).

The custom ASIC platform. A library of blocks dropped into a customer-specified chip, each with a quantified claim from the June 2025 event: custom dense SRAM at 17x the bandwidth per unit area of the best available third-party 1Mb instance, 50% lower area at equal bandwidth and 66% lower standby power; custom HBM base dies releasing 1.7x more useful compute area and cutting memory I/O power 75%; package-integrated voltage regulation cutting total product power 15%; die-to-die interconnect at 10–20 Tbps/mm today with a roadmap to above 50 Tbps/mm [deck slides 91, 95, 97, 98]. Process reach is 5nm in production, 3nm ramping, and 2nm and 1.4nm in development with gate-all-around transistors and back-side power delivery; packaging in use includes CoWoS, InFo and EMIB with 2.5D, 3D and 3.5D interposers (10-K FY2026, Item 1). The commercial consequence of winning this business is a lower gross margin, because more of the bill of materials passes through.

CXL memory expansion and near-memory compute. CXL adds a cache-coherent memory-expansion path over PCIe so memory capacity can grow without adding CPU sockets. Designed for x86 servers before AI, it found a larger application in inference key-value caching, where memory per accelerator scales disproportionately. Five unique custom CXL sockets exist across two Tier 1 US hyperscalers with a third in deep engagement; the first shipped from Q1 FY2026 (Q3 FY2026 call). DDR4 support lets customers reuse prior-generation memory with new accelerators, which is why DRAM scarcity has pulled demand into this category without Marvell changing anything.

Scale-up fabrics with no revenue. Three protocols compete to tie tens to hundreds of accelerators into one coherent domain: UALink (open consortium, spec 1.0 ratified April 2025), Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking, and NVLink opened to third parties through NVLink Fusion. Marvell is building silicon for all three on the Teralynx architecture and 224G SerDes. UALink 115T and 57T were on track to sample in the second half of FY2027 with volume production in FY2028. Hyperscalers wanting rack-level product in early 2026 used Broadcom Tomahawk with a scale-up extension because no UALink silicon existed (theregister.com, accessed 2026-08-28) [web]. Marvell's stated reason customers will choose it is end-to-end ownership of both ends of the link: "especially in scale up, they need to book end the link, and they need to trust it on both sides of it… point solutions at this juncture, we believe are not going to get it done" (Q2 FY2027 call). That is a forward claim with no shipped system behind it.

The roadmap record. Marvell delivers where it controls the whole design and is late where it depends on someone else's ecosystem or entered a category behind an incumbent.

Marvell's differentiation is narrow and deep. It is defensible where the product is a standalone high-speed mixed-signal part sold into a socket Marvell defines. It is weak where the product is a large digital chip competing against an incumbent with more scale — the same 224G SerDes yields roughly 60% share in PAM4 DSPs and roughly 4% in switch silicon.▪ And it is unproven where the value depends on winning three adjacent sockets at once.

3. Competitive advantages and moat assessment

3.1 Data center — custom silicon

Marvell's custom-silicon franchise has a narrow technical advantage and almost no economic one. Three or four firms in the world can take a 2.5D or 3D accelerator from architecture to high-volume production at 3nm with in-house 224G SerDes, hardened Arm compute, dense SRAM, custom HBM interfaces and CoWoS-class packaging. Marvell is one of them, and that capability is why hyperscalers keep awarding it sockets. What the capability has not produced is pricing power.▪ The business earns an estimated 30–44% gross margin, centred near 35–39%, against 63–66% for the standard products sold out of the same IP library, and Marvell's reported non-GAAP gross margin has declined in every year since custom production revenue began: 64.5% in FY2023, 61.0% in FY2025, 59.5% in FY2026, 58.9% in each of the first two quarters of FY2027, and a 58.0% midpoint guided for Q3 FY2027.▪ Management named the custom ramp as the cause of the Q3 step-down. The 64–66% long-term gross-margin model defended through FY2024 no longer appears in the guidance.

The durability test has already run once and Marvell lost it. Marvell designed Amazon's Trainium 2 and lost the following generation.▪ Benchmark downgraded the stock on 2025-12-08 on "a high degree of conviction that the company has lost both Amazon's Trainium3 and 4 designs to its Taiwanese competitor, Alchip", and the shares declined 9% intraday (sherwood.news, accessed 2026-08-28) [web]. SemiAnalysis attributes the loss to Trainium 2 execution, naming a timeline overrun and redistribution-layer interposer problems, and places Alchip on the Trainium 3 back-end physical and package design with Annapurna on the front end [web]. The trade has since shown in reported revenue: Alchip's revenue declined about 40% in 2025 while it sat out the generation it lost, then rose 82.6% sequentially to $241.7m in the June 2026 quarter as N3 accelerator mass production began in late May [web]. Marvell's own slide puts the useful life of an XPU socket at 18 to 24 months. A design win re-competed roughly every seven quarters is not a switching cost.▪

The Google agreement makes the bargaining position explicit. Marvell issued a warrant over 58,970,907 shares, about 6.7% of the share count, vesting one tranche per $500m of custom-product revenue against purchases the 8-K describes as "discretionary", with no minimum volume. The estimated grant-date fair value is $6bn to $10bn, roughly 5% to 8% of the $120bn it vests against, which takes the reported gross margin on Google programmes from a pre-warrant 35% to about 29%-31%. Broadcom has never issued a customer warrant.▪

The consolidated record is the plainest evidence. Across FY2017 to FY2026 Marvell generated $43,096m of revenue and $27m of cumulative GAAP operating income, with operating losses in five of the ten years. FY2026 was the best year in the company's history and produced a 7.4% return on invested capital, below a fabless leading-edge cost of capital of roughly 10–11%. Broadcom earned 17.0% on the same definition in its latest fiscal year and NVIDIA 71.8%.▪ The gross-margin gap to Broadcom has been roughly stable at 16–18 points on a GAAP basis for five years; the operating-margin gap narrowed on the annual comparison, because Broadcom's FY2024 and FY2025 GAAP figures absorb VMware purchase accounting, then widened to 31.8 points on the most recent quarter each company reported.

Management's account, the external account and the industry structure disagree in a specific place, and the structure explains both of the others. Management describes multi-generational engagements, unprecedented design activity, more than twenty sockets and a $10bn-plus FY2029 target. External reporting describes a supplier that lost its anchor programme on execution. The structure fits both: the buyer owns the architecture, the roadmap and the volume; the supplier owns IP blocks, physical implementation and supply chain; each generation is a new bakeoff; and the winner's economics are set by the buyer's alternatives, which now number at least four credible ASIC houses plus the buyers' own silicon teams. Minimum efficient scale lies with the buyer: a hyperscaler placing one 3nm accelerator programme is already at the volume where a second source is economic, and Amazon proved it. Switching costs run the wrong way, because the architecture, instruction set, compiler and software stack belong to the customer while the supplier contributes blocks and implementation. The 10-K states the exit condition: "there may be no other customers for these products due to their custom or semi-custom nature."

Claimed advantage Test it must pass What the evidence shows

Marvell secured 3nm wafer and packaging capacity for a follow-on generation and holds purchase orders covering the FY2027 forecast for a next-generation programme. It also lost the flagship programme's next two generations

Marvell has taken multiple complex custom accelerators to volume production with first-time silicon success and met a steep ramp, which very few firms can do; it defined the XPU-attach category, which reached more than fifteen design wins across several hyperscalers; and it holds a portfolio spanning all three scale-up protocols. Those are real capabilities. None has yet shown up as a margin, a return or a retained generation.

This is not an advantage that has survived well-funded attempts to break it and throws off returns with little reinvestment, because the one attempt to break it succeeded, at Amazon, in 2025. It is not the no-edge case either, because a real technical barrier keeps the field to three or four firms. It earns a position in the middle, toward the lower end: defensible today on execution and IP breadth, open to erosion at every generation boundary, and not yet earning its cost of capital.▪

Business-model analogues. Alchip Technologies (3661.TW) and Global Unichip (3443.TW) are the closest by the shape of the advantage: the same sole-source-per-programme ASIC design-and-turnkey model, the same customer concentration and the same rebid-per-generation exposure, earning 26% and 21.5% gross margins in their last full fiscal years, and 34.8% and 21.5% in their June-quarter 2026 disclosures.▪ The analogue holds on structure and breaks on IP content, because Marvell contributes far more of its own silicon: its modelled 38% custom gross margin is about twelve points above Alchip's last full year and sixteen above GUC's. Celestica (CLS) is the third: a hyperscaler-concentrated programme-win business where the customer owns the architecture and rebids each generation, which is the durability profile exactly; it breaks on value-add, since Celestica has no proprietary silicon and earns roughly 11% gross margins. The useful contrast is Astera Labs (ALAB), which sells PCIe switching, retiming and CXL memory expansion — the functions Marvell markets as XPU attach — as merchant parts to many buyers, and earned a 73.7% non-GAAP gross margin on $392.4m of revenue in the June 2026 quarter.

3.2 Data center — interconnect and merchant silicon

This franchise earns returns above its cost of capital and the source is identifiable: a 224G and 112G SerDes and DSP block that Marvell gets to production earlier than anyone except Broadcom, then reuses across optical DSPs, retimers, AEC DSPs, switch silicon and custom ASICs.▪ Marvell has been first to production at every PAM4 generation from 200G through 1.6T and holds roughly 60% of the 400G-and-above PAM4 DSP market against Broadcom's 30%-plus [web]. That lead produces an estimated 63–66% merchant gross margin and a data-center business that grew 46% year over year in the quarter ended 2026-08-01.

The advantage does not extend to price. The 10-K commits to continued price reductions on existing products, and blended non-GAAP gross margin declined from 64.9% in FY2022 to 58.9% in the quarter ended 2026-08-01, with 57.5–58.5% guided for the October quarter and the same range indicated for FY2028. Management attributes that decline to custom mix, and the estimated merchant-only margin does hold near 64%. But 64% is about six points below Broadcom's semiconductor-segment gross margin of approximately 70% in its April 2026 quarter, below Astera Labs at 73.7% non-GAAP and below Credo at 68.3% non-GAAP in comparable quarters. On like products Marvell's merchant margin sits below Broadcom, Astera Labs and Credo, and the gap to Broadcom has not closed in five years.▪

Scale points the same way. Broadcom's AI networking revenue was roughly $4,300m in its quarter ended 2026-05-03 [estimate: almost 40% of a disclosed $10.8bn of AI semiconductor revenue], roughly twice Marvell's entire data-center revenue of $2,171m in the quarter ended 2026-08-01, and Broadcom ships a 102.4T Ethernet switch in production while Marvell's 51.2T part is in its first volume year. Credo grew revenue 206% in the year to 2026-05-02 and Astera Labs 104% year over year in its June 2026 quarter, both from adjacent connectivity sockets, both at higher gross margins.

Buyer power is the structural limit. Ten customers accounted for 82% of FY2026 revenue, one distributor for 45% of the quarter ended 2026-05-02, and three customers for 75% of gross receivables at that date.▪ Every design win is negotiated against a buyer with the engineering capability to second-source it, dual-source it or build it, and the 10-K says exactly that: "some of our customers have chosen to develop certain semiconductor products internally and this trend may continue to proliferate."

Switching costs are per-socket and expire at each speed transition. A module maker that qualifies a Marvell DSP into an 800G transceiver has sunk firmware, thermal, optical-link and interoperability work and will not swap mid-life; the 10-K describes the effect from the incumbent's side ("If a customer's system designer initially chooses a competitor's product, it becomes significantly more difficult for us to sell our products for use in that system"). The lock lasts one product generation. Every eighteen to twenty-four months the socket is re-tendered at the next speed.▪ Retention in this business is a function of being first to sample the next node, which is what management calls its first-to-market cadence and what Broadcom attacked in March 2026.

Return on invested capital. FY2026 GAAP operating income of $1,323m at a 12.4% effective tax rate gives NOPAT of $1,159m against invested capital of $15,640m (equity $14,308m plus long-term debt $3,971m less cash $2,639m), so 7.4%.

Denominator Invested capital ROIC
As reported $15,640m 7.4%
Excluding $11,062m of goodwill $4,578m 25.3%
Excluding goodwill and $1,755m of acquired intangibles $2,823m 41.1%

The operating business earns well on the capital it currently employs, and the price paid to assemble it absorbed most of the excess. Marvell paid $9,918m for Inphi (closed 2021-04-20 against Inphi's CY2020 revenue of $683m, so 14.5x sales), $1,004m for Innovium and $502m for Aquantia — $11,424m for the IP base of this segment, equal to 73% of FY2026 invested capital. Incremental returns measured from FY2021 to FY2026 are 19.9%: NOPAT moved from −$225m to $1,159m, a change of $1,384m, against a $6,960m increase in invested capital. Extending that measurement to the Q2 FY2027 run rate requires adding back acquired-intangible amortization, which changes the basis, so the two figures are not comparable. On the Q2 FY2027 annualized figure with amortization added back and tax at the guided 13%, as-reported ROIC is roughly 15.5%, above a 10–12% cost of capital for a fabless designer at 1.3x gross leverage; on the FY2026 as-reported basis it was below it. Ongoing capital expenditure is 4.3% of revenue, so growth here needs little further fixed capital; the constraint is capacity prepayments and working capital.

This advantage earns excess returns today and is defensible for now, and it is open to erosion as rivals, customers and packaging architecture shift. Broadcom built a 30%-plus PAM4 DSP position from nothing. The two transitions Marvell itself describes — linear pluggable optics, whose chipset is TIAs and drivers with no DSP, and co-packaged optics, which moves the optical engine onto the switch package where Broadcom owns the switch — both remove or relocate the socket that generates the highest-value content today. Management's own description of the moment is that customers are "evaluating a broad range of potential solutions with multiple technologies under consideration, including NPO and CPO packaging options… as well as 3 different modulator technologies" (Q2 FY2027 call). Marvell's response is to fund all of them, which is the position of a supplier that cannot set the architecture.

Business-model analogues. Analog Devices is the stronger version of the same model: proprietary mixed-signal IP reused across sockets with multi-year design-win lives, earning 61.5% gross and 26.6% operating margins in FY2025. The comparison breaks because ADI sells to thousands of customers where Marvell's interconnect revenue reaches a handful of hyperscalers through one distributor at 45% of sales. MACOM is the weaker version and the closest product match, selling TIAs, drivers and analog into the same optical modules socket by socket at 54.7% gross and 13.4% operating margins in FY2025, differing because MACOM has no DSP or switch silicon and therefore no reusable digital block to amortize. Silicon Motion is the analogue for the storage-controller line: a controller supplier qualified into a handful of NAND and drive makers, earning 48.3% gross and 10.5% operating margins in CY2025, which is what a near-universal component position produces when the buyers are four consolidated OEMs. Marvell falls between ADI and MACOM, closer to ADI on IP depth and closer to MACOM on customer concentration.

3.3 Communications and other

This franchise holds a real but second-tier position that earns no demonstrable excess return, and the part of it with the strongest evidence of a durable edge has already been sold.▪ Enterprise networking is the defensible core: Prestera switch silicon and Alaska PHYs are designed into OEM platforms that live five to ten years, qualification takes months, and the 10-K states that a lost socket is lost for the life of that product. Management's own 2021 gross-margin chart places enterprise networking above the corporate average [deck: 2021-10-06, slide 120]. That lock-in slowed the decline and slowed the recovery, and it produced neither pricing power nor above-market growth. Management's forward growth rate for the business, given on the Q3 FY2026 call, is enterprise IT spending from a base it calls fully normalized at roughly $1bn annualized, 27% below the FY2023 level.

Carrier is worse, and the threat is architectural. Revenue went from $1,084.0m in FY2023 to $338.2m in FY2025, and the nine-month FY2026 recovery to $436.3m was about half the equivalent FY2024 period [web]. Global RAN equipment sales declined about a fifth between 2022 and 2024 and are forecast to compound at 1% a year to 2030 (delloro.com, accessed 2026-08-28) [web], so Marvell's 69% decline ran at roughly 3.1x the market.▪ Both named OCTEON Fusion customers have announced alternatives: NVIDIA invested $1.0bn in Nokia at $6.01 per share on 2025-10-28 alongside AI-RAN products for 5G-Advanced and 6G running on the NVIDIA Arc Aerial RAN Computer (nvidianews.nvidia.com, accessed 2026-08-28) [web], and Samsung is developing its own silicon and using Intel processors for virtualized RAN [web]. Consumer is console and gateway cycle exposure with no defensible position, down from $845.8m in FY2020 to $316.1m in FY2025. The one legally enforced barrier is the Avera-derived US government and defence ASIC work under National Industrial Security Program facility clearances, which a competitor cannot enter without the same clearances, and whose revenue is not disclosed.

Marvell wrote down the roadmap assets in these end markets: the Fiscal 2025 Plan cut new product development outside data center, cancelled future product releases and produced impairment inside $711.8m of restructuring charges after a discounted-cash-flow test showed carrying values were not recoverable. Marvell then sold the best asset in the segment: Infineon paid $2.5bn for the automotive Ethernet business on $225–250m of calendar-2025 revenue at about 60% gross margin, a stated number-one position, eight of the top ten global OEMs and a $4bn lifetime design-win pipeline growing at an expected 25% CAGR — roughly 10x revenue. And the returns are absent. The two public companies whose revenue mix most resembles what is left, Microchip and Semtech, earned 3.6% and 3.3% ROIC in their latest fiscal years on a uniform 15% tax rate, and MACOM, the nearest match for the carrier and defence residue, earned 7.1%, all below a 9–11% cost of capital. Marvell's consolidated GAAP ROIC was negative in every year from FY2020 to FY2025 except FY2023, and this segment supplied 59–69% of revenue in FY2020 through FY2024 before collapsing to 28% in FY2025.

Management's account, the external sources and the industry structure disagree, and the disagreement resolves one way. Management's 2021 claims — gaining share, growing above market, gross margin above the corporate average — are contradicted by the revenue record and by management's own later statements, which put terminal growth at market rates. External sources corroborate a strong position in one sub-market that has since been divested and a deteriorating one in another. The industry structure explains why: entry barriers high enough to keep the supplier list short but low enough to admit several viable suppliers, socket-level switching costs that move share slowly in both directions, concentrated buyers who can and do insource, moderate minimum efficient scale, and continuous price decline. This advantage is defensible for now and open to erosion, and the erosion is already visible in the carrier line and in the company's own capital allocation.

Business-model analogues. Microchip Technology is the closest by shape: broad standard-product silicon designed into long-lived OEM platforms, sold heavily through distribution, protected by socket lock-in and qualification cost, and deeply cyclical. It breaks on concentration, because Microchip's catalogue spans tens of thousands of parts with no 10% customer while Marvell's top ten are 82% of revenue. MACOM is the analogue for the carrier and government residue, earning 7.1% ROIC on a 54.7% gross margin, and breaks on defence weighting, which is a much larger share of MACOM. NXP is the third, earning 14.6% ROIC on standard products into industrial and communications-infrastructure platforms, and breaks because NXP owns fabs and sells into automotive qualification regimes this segment no longer touches.

4. Competitive landscape and market sizing

4.1 Data center — custom silicon

Marvell is the second-largest full-service custom silicon supplier by revenue and runs at a small fraction of Broadcom's. Counterpoint Research puts Broadcom at 60% and Marvell at 8% of 2027 AI-server compute-ASIC design-partner shipments (counterpointresearch.com, accessed 2026-08-28) [web]. Marvell's own target is 20% of a $55bn custom compute market by calendar 2028.▪

The customer is one of six or seven hyperscalers, and each re-bids two separable jobs every generation: architecture and front-end logic design, which the hyperscaler increasingly keeps in house, and the physical implementation, IP, packaging, foundry interface and yielded-part delivery, which it buys. Marvell's 10-K describes the second job and its economics in one sentence: "for certain products we use an ASIC model to offer end-to-end solutions for intellectual property, design team, fab and packaging to deliver a tested, yielded product to customers. This business model tends to have a lower gross margin."

Three structurally different suppliers compete for the same sockets, and the profit pool has moved to whoever owns the reusable IP.

Supplier type Example What it sells Gross margin on that work
Full-service, IP-rich Broadcom SerDes, packaging, switch IP, the whole accelerator plus the networking around it Semiconductor segment approximately 70%, operating margin 62% (quarter ended 2026-05-03)
Full-service, mixed merchant book Marvell The same portfolio at smaller scale, with custom inside a majority-merchant company Not disclosed; estimated 30–44% on custom
Turnkey back-end and design service Alchip, GUC Physical design, package design, wafer and substrate pass-through Alchip 26% FY2025; GUC 21.5% in Q2 CY2026

Alchip's gross margin declined from 34.2% in 2021 to 19.6% in 2024 as production mix rose, then recovered to 26.4% in 2025 because production volume collapsed; GUC's declined from 34.6% in 2021 to 22.8% on the twelve months to June 2026 as turnkey passed 80% of revenue [web]. Production turnkey earns roughly 20%; the design house's margin in any single period is dominated by where its programmes are in the NRE-versus-production cycle.

Who sets price. The hyperscaler, through three observable mechanisms. Per-generation re-bidding: Alchip did the back end for Trainium 1, lost the Trainium 2 generation to Marvell, and regained Trainium 3 on N3 with mass production from late May 2026 [web]. Deliberate multi-sourcing: Google now runs Broadcom, MediaTek and Marvell in parallel. And no purchase commitment in the largest disclosed contract: the Google warrant vests against "discretionary purchases", so the $120bn implied by 240 tranches of $500m is a vesting ceiling, not an order.▪

Peer scale and KPI comparison. Scale here is set by custom silicon revenue, hyperscaler programmes in volume production, contracted forward revenue and the leading node qualified for production. Total company revenue misleads: Broadcom's is a third software, MediaTek's mostly smartphone, Socionext's mostly automotive and industrial.

Marvell leads the field on the breadth of the attach portfolio: it defined the category, holds above fifteen attach wins including five CXL sockets across two Tier-1 US hyperscalers, and has line of sight to above $2bn from NIC and CXL alone by FY2029. No design-service house competes there.▪ Marvell trails Broadcom on accelerator revenue by roughly an order of magnitude, on customer count by six to two, and on disclosed forward commitments, where Broadcom publishes a $73bn AI backlog and named gigawatt agreements at four customers. MediaTek is closing ground fastest, from nothing to a $2bn 2026 target [web].

Share arithmetic. Pairing Marvell fiscal years with the overlapping Broadcom years, and taking Broadcom's XPU revenue at 60% of its disclosed AI semiconductor revenue (the low end of the 60–65% band it has given across four quarters):

Period Marvell custom Broadcom XPU [estimate] Marvell share of the pair
MRVL FY2026 vs AVGO FY2025 $1.5bn ~$12bn ~11%

[estimate: management's own custom figures and growth guides against Broadcom's disclosed AI revenue at a 60% XPU share; precision is one significant figure because the Broadcom split is a band and the FY2027 Marvell figure spans the written ">20%" guide and the ~$2.5bn implied by the data-center identity]. Both this measure and Counterpoint's 8% shipment share are far below the 20% Marvell targets for calendar 2028.

The dollar target and the share target stop agreeing once the market is sized bottom-up. Summing supplier-level CY2027 custom revenue — Broadcom above $60bn, MediaTek multi-billion, Marvell about $4bn, Alchip $2–6bn, GUC about $2bn, Socionext under $1bn — gives roughly $75–80bn for CY2027, against Marvell's published $55bn for CY2028 [estimate: sum of supplier guides and estimates; the Alchip row is a sell-side unit build and is the widest input]. Against that, $10bn of FY2029 custom revenue is roughly 8–10% share, close to Counterpoint's figure and under half the company target. Marvell can hit the dollar target and miss the share target by more than half.▪

Counter-evidence, ordered by how much each changes the structure.

  • The AWS flagship socket changed design partners after one generation. Alchip did Trainium 1, Marvell won Trainium 2 on 5nm, Alchip won Trainium 3 on N3 and entered mass production in late May 2026, with Annapurna holding the front-end design [web]. Asked directly in August 2025 whether the 3nm follow-on was still Marvell's, Murphy declined: "commenting on just the individual sockets at this point is only probably increasing the noise level." By March 2026 an analyst framed the same programme on the call as "a very strong start, followed by competition from another supplier" and the premise went unchallenged. Alchip's total revenue declined about 40% in 2025 while it was out of the generation it lost, which puts a maximum on the socket, because Alchip has other HPC and networking customers.
  • Front-end design is moving in house. On Trainium 3 the front end and the majority mask set belong to Annapurna [web]. The 10-K names the trend, and a new FY2026 risk factor extends it: "AI-driven design tools may lower traditional barriers to entry in the semiconductor industry by enabling new market participants… to develop high-performance, custom semiconductor solutions in-house."
  • MediaTek entered from zero and is scaling faster than Marvell. Google TPU v7e into risk production by end-Q1 2026, v8e ordered, a $2bn AI ASIC revenue target for calendar 2026 doubled from $1bn three months earlier, a 10–15% 2027 share target, and $5bn committed to the AI data center business [web]. MediaTek's 2026 target is roughly the size of Marvell's whole FY2027 custom business.▪
  • NVIDIA occupies three positions at once. It is named as a competitor in the FY2026 10-K, holds $2.0bn of Marvell Series A Convertible Preferred issued 2026-03-31 convertible into up to 21,778,000 shares, and is an NVLink Fusion interoperability partner. The merchant GPU also sets the price ceiling for every custom programme: both Marvell and Broadcom describe hyperscalers producing their own accelerators at roughly 40% of the cost of merchant GPUs while renting them at 60–70% of GPU prices [web].

Contradictions in the market sizing. Marvell published a $40bn custom XPU market for CY2028 in June 2025. Broadcom guides to more than $100bn of AI semiconductor revenue in its fiscal year ending November 2027, of which roughly 60% is accelerator silicon on its own disclosure, so above $60bn from one supplier a year earlier. Broadcom's CEO characterises that revenue as silicon content; Marvell's market estimate excludes HBM, which the largest hyperscalers buy directly. Part of the gap is definitional and neither company publishes the reconciliation. Separately, management describes the customer base as diversified — "we're quite diversified across each of them… we're highly diversified within each of these customers" (Q4 FY2026 call) — over a period in which the largest distributor moved from 24% of revenue in FY2024 to 45% in Q1 FY2027. The claim measures product breadth inside an account; the disclosure measures revenue by account.

4.2 Data center — interconnect and merchant silicon

Marvell is the scale leader in high-speed optical DSPs and pluggable coherent modules and a distant challenger in the other three lines inside this segment.▪ Against its own market map it held roughly 35–40% of the data-center interconnect market and roughly 4% of merchant Ethernet switching in FY2026 [estimate: Marvell line revenue over Marvell's own CY-interpolated market sizes]. Broadcom is widening the gap fastest, and NVIDIA's data-center networking revenue of $14,800m in the quarter ended 2026-04-26 was 8.1x Marvell's whole data-center segment in the near-coincident quarter.

Each of the four lines is a two- or three-firm market at the high end, and Marvell occupies a different position in each.

Marvell is the third entrant into a copper market Credo defined and Astera industrialised: Credo did $1.3bn and Astera is running above $1.5bn annualized while Marvell's combined AEC and retimer revenue has never been sized.▪ In switching the business tripled off a small base and remains under 5% of its own defined market. Management does not contest this. On the Q1 FY2027 call an analyst said "I know it's a large market and you have relatively small share in that market", and Murphy's answer redirected to scale-up, "where the market share isn't established yet."

Where the value migrates next, and who decides. Two mechanisms move the profit pool away from the standalone pluggable module. Linear pluggable optics removes the DSP from the module and leaves Marvell selling the TIA and driver, which it also makes, at lower dollar content. Co-packaged optics moves the photonics onto the switch or accelerator substrate, where the switch vendor specifies who supplies it.▪ Broadcom's published figure for its Bailly co-packaged part is 5W of optical interconnect power per 800Gbps against roughly 14W for a DSP pluggable [web, unverified], and the first commercial scale-out co-packaged deployments in 2026 are on Broadcom platforms. Adoption of linear pluggable optics has been slower than the early forecasts: the IEEE Electronics Packaging Society's March 2026 overview states that "adoption remains limited, especially at 800G due to entrenched DSP-based infrastructure" and recommends linear-receive optics over linear pluggable at 1.6T (eps.ieee.org, accessed 2026-08-28) [web]. Marvell's answer is to sell the switch as well as the optics, which requires winning a switching contest it has already lost once in scale-out.

Contradictions. Marvell states its Bravera HDD controllers "are being used by all the current HDD makers", wording unchanged across the FY2022 through FY2026 10-Ks, while Seagate disclosed selling its SoC intellectual property, equipment and design assets to a Broadcom subsidiary on 2024-04-23 for $600m and restructuring pre-existing purchasing agreements (STX 10-K FY2026). Both can hold at once, and the unchanged wording does not reflect the change in who designs the largest drive maker's SoCs. On DSP share, two trade sources give 60% and 70% for the same quantity, and a top-down derivation against Marvell's own market map gives 35–40% of the broader interconnect market on a wider denominator; the spread is not resolvable from public material. And Marvell guides interconnect to above 70% growth in FY2027 while describing itself as gaining share, in a period when Broadcom's AI networking, NVIDIA's data-center networking, Credo and Astera all grew faster than 70%. Both statements can hold only if the market itself is growing faster than 70%.

4.3 Communications and other

Marvell is not the scale leader in any of the four businesses inside this segment. In enterprise networking and carrier it is the second merchant supplier behind Broadcom, whose non-AI semiconductor revenue at its fiscal-2024 trough was roughly 8x this whole segment. In consumer it is smaller than Silicon Motion, a controller-only supplier whose $451.0m of revenue in the June 2026 quarter alone exceeded Marvell's estimated full-year consumer revenue. In what remains of automotive and industrial it holds roughly $125m of industrial Ethernet, video surveillance and US government ASIC revenue after the Infineon divestiture [estimate: the retained residual after solving the divested automotive line out of the Q2-to-Q3 FY2026 step-down].

Marvell is the second-largest merchant supplier in enterprise networking and the only member of that merchant group whose latest full-year revenue is below its FY2022 level. In carrier, vendor concentration among the five RAN suppliers reached a ten-year high in 2025 and two of the five are Chinese and design their own baseband, which leaves Marvell three serviceable customers, of which two have announced alternatives.

Market sizing, tested against outcomes. Marvell's October 2021 investor day sized its serviceable market at $20bn in CY2021 growing to $30bn in CY2024, with enterprise, on-premise, wired and industrial at $7.9bn growing to $8.8bn (4% CAGR) and consumer at $1.5bn growing to $1.8bn (6% CAGR) [deck: 2021-10-06, slide 17]. Against the $9.4bn CY2021 base, Marvell's FY2022 revenue from those lines of $1,857.3m implies roughly 20% share; against the $10.6bn CY2024 base, the FY2025 equivalent of $1,264.9m implies about 12% [estimate: Marvell's own market slide against its own reported end-market revenue, with a January fiscal year mapped to the prior calendar year]. The FY2022 base was inflated by shortage-era double-ordering and the FY2025 base deflated by the inventory correction, so the underlying trend lies inside that range and equals neither endpoint. The same deck folded 5G into a 20%-CAGR bucket alongside cloud; the RAN market Marvell sells into instead lost about a fifth of its value between 2022 and 2024 and is forecast at 1% compound growth through 2030 [web].

Counter-evidence, ordered by how much each changes the structure. Nokia moving its next radio generation to NVIDIA compute is the largest identified socket in the carrier line and it is now challenged by a supplier that is simultaneously Marvell's data-center partner and a $2.0bn preferred holder. Cisco's in-house campus silicon takes the largest campus port volumes out of the merchant pool, and Cisco has been a named Marvell competitor in every 10-K since FY2022. Marvell's own withdrawal of investment matters on a multi-year lag: the FY2025 restructuring cancelled future product releases here, and design wins secured in FY2025 and FY2026 determine revenue in FY2028 through FY2030. And management's own framing claims no share gain: enterprise networking will grow "in line with enterprise IT spending" from a roughly $1bn annualized base, and carrier will settle into growth "in line with carrier capex" (Q3 FY2026 call).

Marvell earns a lower gross margin than the foundry that fabricates its chips. On the non-GAAP measure it is about nine points below both TSMC and Broadcom, sixteen below NVIDIA, seventeen below Astera Labs and twenty-six below Micron.▪ Of the silicon-design layers, Marvell is the least profitable per dollar of revenue; only assembly and test, optical modules, photonic contract manufacture and system build earn less.

How much of the hyperscaler dollar Marvell captures. Combined trailing-twelve-month infrastructure capital expenditure at Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta was $506.7bn. Alphabet discloses that about 60% of its technical infrastructure assets were servers and network equipment at 2025-12-31; applying that share to all four gives a silicon-bearing base of roughly $304bn [estimate: Alphabet's disclosed 60% server share applied to the four buyers' total capex]. Marvell's data-center revenue for the twelve months to 2026-08-01 was $7,173m, which is 1.4% of the total capex figure and 2.4% of the server-and-network slice.▪ That data-center line also includes storage OEMs, on-premise enterprise, telco DCI and third-party module makers, none of which are hyperscaler capex, so at two-thirds attribution the figure is 1.6%. Marvell captures 1.6% to 2.4% of the hyperscaler server-and-network dollar.

Where the constraint binds. Advanced packaging and substrate bind before wafers, and memory has become a second binding point.▪ The FY2026 10-K describes the FY2023 episode by name: "supply shortages in the semiconductor industry of multi-layer complex substrates, IC packaging capacity, and specific wafer process node constraints resulted in increased lead times, inability to meet demand, and increased costs." The Q2 FY2027 release lists as a principal risk "constrained supply or limited availability of advanced semiconductor wafers, substrates, outsourced test services, and other electronic components" — outsourced test appearing alongside wafers and substrates points at the assembly-and-test layer. Independent capacity work supports the same location: Epoch AI estimates that NVIDIA, Google, AMD and Amazon together consumed over 90% of global chip-on-wafer-on-substrate packaging capacity and about 90% of HBM by value in 2025 while taking only about 12% of advanced logic die production, and it describes logic fabrication as "a softer constraint" (epoch.ai, accessed 2026-08-28) [web].

Marvell's own new deposits show where the constraint binds. The Q1 FY2027 10-Q states that after 2026-05-02 Marvell "entered into agreements to secure wafer and substrate manufacturing capacity through fiscal years 2030 and 2033, respectively," with deposits totalling $870.0m payable quarterly from Q2 FY2027 through Q2 FY2028. Marvell reserved substrate three years further into the future than silicon.

Memory is where the constraint now prices. Micron's gross margin was 84.6% in the quarter ended 2026-05-28 on revenue of $41.46bn against $9.30bn a year earlier, and it expects margins under its "strategic customer agreements with price bands, even at floor pricing levels, to yield gross margins well above our peak quarterly margins in any past cycle." That matters to Marvell directly, because custom HBM is part of its custom accelerator platform, and memory bought at an 85% supplier gross margin and passed through a custom programme compresses Marvell's own reported margin dollar for dollar. Marvell has said the largest hyperscalers buy HBM directly, so the exposure is in the emerging-hyperscaler turnkey programmes, and no programme-level disclosure exists.

Who is locking up whom. Marvell places firm orders with suppliers up to 26 weeks before delivery and makes further supply commitments up to 52 weeks; capacity reservation agreements run four to ten years.

Disclosed in Purchase commitments, total Next fiscal year Beyond next fiscal year
10-K FY2023 $3,147.1m $742.7m $2,404.4m
10-K FY2024 $2,431.1m $820.5m $1,610.6m
10-K FY2025 $1,638.4m $1,021.9m $616.5m
10-K FY2026 $2,665.8m $1,871.8m $794.0m
10-Q Q1 FY2027 $2,756.8m $2,265.2m (remainder of FY2027) $491.6m

The near-dated obligation is at a record and rising fast — $2,265.2m committed for the remaining three quarters of FY2027 against $742.7m for the whole of FY2024 four years earlier. The obligation beyond twelve months is at a multi-year low of $491.6m, while management guides custom revenue to more than double in FY2028 and reach $10bn or more annually in FY2029. Marvell buys firm capacity for the next four quarters and declines to commit firm volume beyond that.▪ The $870.0m of new deposits changes the structure and not the duration: they reserve capacity through FY2030 and FY2033 without becoming purchase-level commitments, so the cash cost lands early and the volume risk does not. Fees and refundable deposits under the reservation arrangements were $99.0m in the FY2023 10-K and $11.5m at Q1 FY2027; the $870.0m agreed one quarter later is 75x that figure.

The precedent runs the other way on how binding these are. In Q1 and Q2 of FY2025 Marvell "worked with its foundry and test and assembly suppliers to amend certain manufacturing supply capacity reservation agreements, which resulted in reducing the Company's related purchase level commitments" — from $2.0bn to $544.6m (10-K FY2025, Note 8). When demand missed, the suppliers took a $1.5bn reduction.

Bargaining power at the customer interface. Distributor A was 24% of FY2024 revenue, 34% FY2025, 37% FY2026 and 45% in Q1 FY2027; Direct Customer A moved from under 10% to 16% over the same span; top-ten customers were 82% of FY2026 revenue; three customers were 75% of gross accounts receivable at 2026-05-02. Against that, Marvell holds almost nothing enforceable: "We typically sell products pursuant to purchase orders rather than long-term purchase commitments. Some of our customers have, and others may in the future, cancel or defer purchase orders on short notice without incurring a significant penalty." Marvell commits 26 to 52 weeks of firm supply and $870.0m of deposits reaching to FY2033 while the demand behind it is cancellable.

Marvell also pays customers in its own equity, booked against revenue. At roughly 6% of qualifying revenue, the Google warrant reduces Google's effective cash price for the silicon by about that amount while giving Google a claim on the supplier's upside, and it is recorded as a reduction of revenue.

Customer-side economics. Depreciable lives for the servers holding Marvell silicon are six years at Alphabet and Amazon, 5.5 years at Meta (extended in January 2025, which cut 2025 depreciation by $2.92bn) and two to six years at Microsoft. Marvell's own roadmap moves faster: 5nm in production, 3nm ramping, 2nm and 1.4nm in development, roughly a two-year node step, so an accelerator held six years on the buyer's books spans three Marvell process generations.

The buyers are funding the marginal dollar with something other than operating cash. Amazon's free cash flow for the twelve months to 2026-06-30 was negative $7,604m — operating cash flow of $161,403m against $169,007m of property and equipment purchases — against positive $18,184m a year earlier (AMZN 10-Q, Q2 CY2026). Alphabet raised aggregate net proceeds of $49.6bn in June 2026 through a common-stock offering and 6.25% mandatory convertible preferred, plus a $40.0bn at-the-market programme, stated as being for "general corporate purposes, including capital expenditures to scale AI infrastructure and global compute" (GOOGL 10-Q, Q2 CY2026). Meta issued $24.91bn of senior unsecured notes in May 2026 and held $349.31bn of non-cancelable contractual commitments at 2026-06-30 (META 10-Q, Q2 CY2026). Marvell's own filings name the same exposure: "the current level of capital expenditure (capex) on AI infrastructure may not be sustainable over the long term and a significant reduction in AI-related spending will likely harm our financial results."

Circular financing. Three flows now cross the chain in both directions and roughly offset in size. NVIDIA put $2.0bn of cash into Marvell on 2026-03-31 for convertible preferred exchangeable into up to 21,778,000 shares at about $91.8355, while being named as a competitor in the same fiscal year's 10-K. Marvell issued Google a warrant over up to 58,970,907 shares that Google earns by buying from Marvell. And Marvell committed $870.0m of deposits and roughly $1bn of FY2027 prepayments to its suppliers. The $2.0bn raised from a competitor roughly funds the supplier prepayments and the buyback, and Marvell's cash rose from $2,638.8m at 2026-01-31 to $3,932.8m at 2026-08-01.

One presentation item flatters the cash line. Marvell sells trade receivables without recourse and presents the proceeds inside operating cash flow: $335.7m sold in FY2024, $868.8m in FY2025, $735.5m in FY2026 and $300.9m in Q1 FY2027 alone. At 2026-05-02, $295.8m remained subject to servicing against $108.5m at 2026-01-31. The same 10-K describes the arrangement two ways — elective liquidity management in the MD&A, and a dependency whose withdrawal "could adversely impact" operating results in the risk factors.

6. Secular and industry trends

Management describes Marvell as a custom AI silicon company gaining share in a data-center market compounding at 35%. The realized numbers do not support that description.

Over the window management itself forecast in 2021, the driver did not appear. The October 2021 investor day forecast Marvell's served market at $20bn in CY2021 growing to $30bn in CY2024, a 13% CAGR, and set a 15–20% long-term revenue CAGR target. Marvell's revenue over exactly that window compounded at 7.5% on the company's own pro-forma FY2022 basis of $4,638m, and 8.9% as reported, to $5,767m in FY2025.▪ Both are below the 13% projected for the market and well below the company target. Marvell's revenue as a proportion of its own defined served market declined from 23.2% to 19.2% over those three years.

In the AI window Marvell grew more slowly than four of the six peers in its own cohort. Growth in the most recently completed fiscal year for each AI-connectivity and custom-silicon peer:

The FY2027 and FY2028 guides do change that: FY2025 to a guided ~$18bn in FY2028 is a 46% three-year CAGR. The acceleration begins in FY2026, six quarters after the AI capex cycle began.

The residual, which contains the PAM4 DSP franchise management calls market-leading, grew about 32% in the year LightCounting puts Ethernet optical transceiver sales up 82% (lightcounting.com, accessed 2026-08-28) [web]. Marvell either lost DSP share, or sold into a mix whose dollar content per module declined, or both.▪ The FY2027 guide of above 70% interconnect growth is roughly in line with LightCounting's 65% forecast for the same calendar period, which is a maintain.

Cyclical against secular. Two cycles run in opposite phase. Communications and other went from a $3,511m FY2023 peak to a $1,603m FY2025 trough and recovered to $2,094m, still 40% below the peak three and a half years later, with new-product investment cut in the FY2025 restructuring and the first sequential decline of the recovery landing in Q2 FY2027.
